meta.title: Who really said "Great minds discuss ideas; average minds discuss events; small minds discuss people"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No, Eleanor Roosevelt never said it. Quote Investigator traces the idea to historian Henry Thomas Buckle (recorded 1901); the modern wording is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Great minds discuss ideas; average minds discuss events; small minds discuss people'?
meta.ogDescription: Eleanor Roosevelt has no documented source for this line. The idea traces to Henry Thomas Buckle, recorded in an 1901 memoir; the wording is a later folk evolution.

answer.label: Not Eleanor Roosevelt — the idea traces to Henry Thomas Buckle
answer.authorDates: 1821–1862 · English historian, author of “History of Civilization in England”
answer.sourceLine: There is no documented instance of Eleanor Roosevelt ever saying or writing this line, and Quote Investigator found no supporting citation for her — the credit only surfaced in newspapers around 1987. The earliest strong match is a conversational maxim attributed to historian Henry Thomas Buckle, recalled in Charles Stewart’s 1901 autobiography Haud Immemor; the crisp modern wording (with “events” in place of “things”) is a later, anonymous evolution of that thought.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from
source.excerpt: Men and women range themselves into three classes or orders of intelligence; you can tell the lowest class by their habit of always talking about persons; the next by the fact that their habit is always to converse about things; the highest by their preference for the discussion of ideas.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the earliest strong match to Charles Stewart’s 1901 autobiography Haud Immemor, where the three-tier hierarchy is credited to historian Henry Thomas Buckle.

The maxim evolved over decades — an 1888 sermon already used “persons, things, events,” and by 1931 a version with “events” appeared in The New York Times’ Queries and Answers column with no author named.
Laurence J. Peter printed the now-standard wording in Peter’s Quotations (1977); newspapers only began attaching Eleanor Roosevelt’s name to it around 1987, and no citation to her was ever found.
source.excerptNote: Charles Stewart’s 1901 recollection of Henry Thomas Buckle’s dinner-table remark — the earliest strong match. Note it speaks of “persons,” “things,” and “ideas,” not the tidy modern “people / events / ideas” triad later pinned on Eleanor Roosevelt.
source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording is an anonymous, gradually evolved paraphrase with no single authored source, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. The closest documented antecedent — Charles Stewart’s Haud Immemor (1901), phrased quite differently — is itself old enough to be public domain, but that is not the wording quoted here.

author.name: Henry Thomas Buckle
author.heading: About Henry Thomas Buckle
author.bio: Henry Thomas Buckle was a self-taught English historian best known for his ambitious, unfinished History of Civilization in England (1857–1861), which sought to place history on a scientific footing. A celebrated conversationalist and one of the strongest amateur chess players of his day, he died young of typhoid fever in 1862. The three-tier “great minds / average minds / small minds” hierarchy is credited to him in a dinner-table recollection published decades after his death.

misattribution.heading: How Eleanor Roosevelt got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable misattributions — a polished aphorism pinned on a beloved public figure with no source behind it.

items.why: Endlessly circulated on quote sites, mugs, and social media as her line, but Quote Investigator found no supporting citation in her speeches or writings; the credit only appears in newspapers from about 1987, decades after her death in 1962.
The three-part “ideas / things / persons” hierarchy is credited to Buckle in Charles Stewart’s 1901 memoir Haud Immemor — the earliest strong match, though in different words from the modern version.
The line is sometimes attached to Socrates or other sages to lend it gravitas, but there is no basis for any of these; the wording is far too modern and no ancient or authored source contains it.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: Eleanor Roosevelt almost certainly never said it — the idea belongs to Henry Thomas Buckle (recorded 1901) and the familiar wording is an anonymous 20th-century evolution, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The saying survives because it flatters the listener: it offers a tidy moral hierarchy and quietly places whoever repeats it among the “great minds.” That built-in appeal, plus a famous name attached to it, is exactly the recipe for a viral misquote.

Its real history is messier and more interesting than the meme — a Victorian dinner-party remark, credited to a historian, gradually smoothed and re-worded over a century until it landed on Eleanor Roosevelt.
context.pull: The version everyone quotes is a century of paraphrase — not a sentence anyone can show Eleanor Roosevelt writing.
